title: “HANNAH’S HUSBAND ASKED, ‘AM I NOT MORE TO YOU THAN TEN SONS?’”
paragraphs: “HANNAH’S HUSBAND ASKED, ‘AM I NOT MORE TO YOU THAN TEN SONS?’”
He loved her. He gave her more. He tried to comfort her. And still Hannah cried—because sometimes being deeply loved does not make the thing you lost hurt any less.
There is a sentence in the Bible that sounds tender until you realize it was spoken to a woman who could barely eat.
A husband looked across the table at the woman he loved.
She was crying again.
Food sat in front of her, untouched.
Around her were the sounds of a family she desperately wanted to have for herself. Children. Voices. Movement. Life.
And somewhere nearby was Peninnah—the woman who possessed the very thing Hannah had prayed for and who knew exactly how to press that wound until it bled.
Then Elkanah asked Hannah:
“Hannah, why weepest thou? and why eatest thou not? and why is thy heart grieved? am not I better to thee than ten sons?”
—1 Samuel 1:8, KJV
In Hebrew, the final question reads:
הֲלוֹא אָנֹכִי טוֹב לָךְ מֵעֲשָׂרָה בָּנִים
Halo anokhi tov lakh me'asarah banim?
Literally, the thought is essentially:
“Am I not better/good to you than ten sons?”
The Hebrew word טוֹב — tov carries the ordinary sense of “good” or “better” in this comparison.
But perhaps the most heartbreaking thing about the question is that Elkanah was not Hannah's enemy.
He loved her.
That matters.
Scripture tells us so.
He gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her. He saw her tears. He noticed she was not eating. He recognized that something inside his wife was breaking.
He cared.
And yet...
he could not become the answer to every ache inside her.
Maybe that is why this ancient scene feels painfully modern.
Because perhaps you have had someone love you and still not understand why you hurt.
Maybe someone has told you:
“But you have so much to be thankful for.”
“You have a good family.”
“You have a husband.”
“You have a wife.”
“You have a job.”
“You have a roof over your head.”
“Other people have it worse.”
“Why are you still sad?”
And everything they said may have been true...
except for the conclusion they expected you to reach.
Because gratitude and grief can live in the same heart.
You can love what God has given you and still grieve what you do not have.
You can worship God and still cry.
You can believe God is good while admitting that something hurts terribly.
You can be surrounded by blessings and still carry one empty room inside your soul that nobody else seems able to enter.
Hannah did.
And Scripture does not mock her for it.
The Bible does not flatten her into a motivational slogan.
It lets her weep.
That matters more than some Christians realize.
Hannah's suffering was not merely that she had no child.
Her pain had acquired a voice.
Peninnah.
Scripture says her rival provoked her severely because of her barrenness.
And then Scripture adds three devastating words:
“year by year.”
Not one terrible afternoon.
Not one insensitive comment.
Year.
After year.
After year.
Imagine arriving at worship already knowing what is coming.
Imagine preparing to seek God while carrying the dread that someone is going to remind you of the prayer God has not answered.
Imagine watching Peninnah's children growing while your own arms remain empty.
Another year.
Another journey to Shiloh.
Another sacrifice.
Another prayer.
Another reminder.
Another tear.
There are wounds that hurt once.
Then there are wounds that wake up every morning with you.
Maybe yours is infertility.
Maybe miscarriage.
Maybe the child you buried.
Maybe the marriage that collapsed.
Maybe the person who promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe the son who no longer calls.
Maybe the daughter who walked away from God.
Maybe the diagnosis you never expected.
Maybe the ministry that failed.
Maybe the addiction you thought you had conquered.
Maybe the financial pressure nobody knows about.
Maybe you smile in church because explaining the truth would take too long.
Maybe you have learned how to worship while bleeding.
Hannah would understand.
And here is something astonishing.
Elkanah asks:
“Am I not better to thee than ten sons?”
But Hannah does not answer him in the recorded text.
She gets up.
And she goes to God.
That may be one of the most important movements in the entire chapter.
Because there comes a moment when human comfort reaches its boundary.
A husband can love you without being able to heal you.
A wife can hold you without being able to rescue you.
A friend can listen without possessing the answer.
A pastor can pray with you without controlling tomorrow.
People can sit beside your wound.
Only God can be God.
Hannah rises and goes before the LORD.
And then Scripture gives us words almost too raw to read casually:
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.”
—1 Samuel 1:10, KJV
The Hebrew describes her as:
מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — marat nephesh
A woman bitterly distressed in her very being.
This was not polished prayer.
This was not religious performance.
This was not Hannah trying to impress the people standing nearby.
She was shattered.
So she prayed shattered.
Her lips moved.
Her voice could not be heard.
Tears were saying what sentences could not.
And then, as though Peninnah's cruelty were not enough, even the priest misunderstood her.
Eli watched her mouth moving and concluded she was drunk.
Think about that.
She came into the presence of God wounded...
and was misjudged by a religious leader while she was praying.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You finally tried to reach for God, and somebody misunderstood you.
You were struggling, and people called you rebellious.
You were exhausted, and somebody called you lazy.
You were grieving, and somebody told you your faith was weak.
You were trying to survive, and someone judged the way survival looked on you.
Hannah finally answered Eli:
“I... have poured out my soul before the LORD.”
That is the line.
That is where hiding ends.
She poured it out.
Not part of it.
Not the church-safe version.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the sentence that makes everybody comfortable.
Her soul.
Before the LORD.
And perhaps that is what somebody needs to hear today:
God is not frightened by the prayer you are afraid to pray.
You do not need to clean up your tears before bringing them to Him.
You do not need to pretend disappointment is victory.
You do not need to call pain “peace” to prove you have faith.
Bring Him the real thing.
The jealousy.
The confusion.
The exhaustion.
The anger you are ashamed to admit.
The question you keep swallowing.
The prayer you stopped praying because another unanswered year felt unbearable.
Pour it out.
Not because God owes us whatever we request.
Hannah's story must never be twisted into a formula that says, “Cry hard enough and God will give you exactly what you want.”
Scripture does not teach that.
Faithful believers sometimes receive the thing they begged God for.
Faithful believers sometimes do not.
Paul pleaded about his thorn and received sustaining grace rather than removal.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane, “not my will, but thine, be done.”
Biblical faith is not forcing God's hand.
Biblical faith places our trembling hand into His.
Hannah asked specifically.
Boldly.
Desperately.
But notice what happened next.
Before Samuel entered her arms...
something happened to Hannah's face.
After Eli spoke peace over her, Scripture says:
“So the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.”
—1 Samuel 1:18, KJV
Do not rush past that.
Samuel had not been born.
Hannah was not pregnant yet.
Her circumstances had not visibly changed.
Peninnah had not vanished.
There was no positive pregnancy test waiting at home.
There was no baby crying in her arms.
Yet Hannah got up...
ate...
and her face was no longer as it had been.
Something changed before the circumstance changed.
She had poured out what she could no longer carry alone.
That does not mean every grieving believer will immediately feel emotionally better after praying. Scripture never turns prayer into a mechanical switch for human emotion.
But Hannah's story shows us something beautiful:
there can be surrender before there is an answer.
There can be worship before there is evidence.
There can be peace while the womb is still empty.
And then came morning.
Do you know what Hannah and Elkanah did before going home?
They worshiped.
That might be one of the most beautiful acts in the chapter.
Hannah worshiped the God who had not yet placed Samuel in her arms.
That is faith.
Not pretending.
Not bargaining.
Not denying reality.
Worship.
Then Scripture says something that echoes throughout the Bible:
“the LORD remembered her.”
This does not mean God had forgotten Hannah and suddenly recovered the memory.
When Scripture speaks this way, God's “remembering” points to His turning toward someone according to His covenant purpose and acting on their behalf.
The God who seemed silent had never been absent.
And in time Hannah conceived.
A boy was born.
Samuel.
The child she had cried for became the child she would surrender back to God.
That is where Hannah's story becomes even more challenging.
Because many of us want God to give us something.
Hannah received what she asked for...
and then released Samuel into God's service according to her vow.
The gift did not replace the Giver.
Her answered prayer became an offering.
And perhaps that is where this story reaches beyond infertility and reaches every one of us.
What if the thing you are asking God for eventually arrives?
Will it become your god?
Or will it become something you can place back into God's hands?
The relationship.
The healing.
The opportunity.
The business.
The platform.
The child.
The ministry.
The money.
The restored life.
Hannah teaches us to pray for the gift without worshiping the gift.
And centuries later, another promised Son would enter the story of humanity.
Not Samuel.
Jesus Christ.
Samuel would become a prophet used mightily by God.
But Samuel could not carry the sin of the world.
Jesus could.
Hannah's empty arms eventually held a son.
But humanity's deeper emptiness required the Son.
Jesus Christ entered our grief, our shame, our rebellion, our death.
He was misunderstood.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And on that cross He bore sin—not because humanity had finally become worthy, but because God is rich in mercy.
This is where every human scandal meets grace.
Our scandal is deeper than what others did to us.
It includes what sin has done within us.
We have sinned.
We have hidden.
We have worshiped created things.
We have wounded others.
We have tried to become our own gods.
And Christianity's answer is not:
“Try harder.”
It is Christ.
The sinless Son of God crucified for sinners and risen from the dead.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously He takes it.
Grace is God offering forgiveness and reconciliation through Jesus Christ to sinners who could never rescue themselves.
So perhaps your deepest need today is not for God to give you your “Samuel.”
Perhaps your deepest need is Jesus.
And even if the prayer you desperately want answered remains unanswered tonight...
Christ is still enough to save you.
Christ is still worthy.
Christ is still risen.
Christ is still merciful.
Christ still receives sinners who come to Him.
Your unanswered prayer does not cancel the cross.
Your tears do not frighten Him.
Your past does not surprise Him.
Your shame is not stronger than His grace.
Your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Maybe you have spent years trying to appear strong.
Stop performing before God.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent where you need to repent.
Confess what you have hidden.
Bring Him what hurts.
Trust Christ with what you cannot repair.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Someone who cries after everybody sleeps.
Someone whose prayer seems unanswered.
Someone who thinks God has forgotten their name.
Put this on your profile where they might find it.
It does not.
Not because money buys salvation, spiritual favor, answered prayer, or a place in God's family.
It never could.
Give freely, prayerfully, and without compulsion.

But if you believe this ministry is bearing Gospel fruit, voluntarily supporting it is one practical way you can help us keep creating, publishing, expanding, and placing Christ-centered resources before people who desperately need them.
It helps us write.
Publish.
Reach.
Teach.
Encourage.
And continue building resources for believers who are hungry to go deeper into Scripture.
You can still help tremendously.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone hurting.
Because ministry is not ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
And perhaps somewhere tonight...
there is another Hannah sitting silently in a crowded room.
Loved...
but hurting.
Blessed...
but grieving.
Surrounded...
but lonely.
Trying to understand why God seems to be answering everybody else's prayer.
Maybe nobody around her understands.
Maybe even the person who loves her most keeps asking why she cannot simply be happy with what she already has.
But Heaven is not intimidated by the prayer she cannot say aloud.
God sees the moving lips.
God sees the untouched food.
God sees the years.
God sees the provocation.
God sees the private tears.
And whether His answer comes in the form she desperately hopes for or through sustaining grace she never expected, she can entrust herself to the God revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
So pour out your soul.
Then place it in His hands.
You may not know what God will write on the next page.
But because of Jesus, you can know that sin, shame, suffering, and death do not get the final word.
Sometimes the prayer that begins with an empty heart becomes the place where you discover that Christ was holding you before your answer ever arrived.
